From St. John, N.B., dated June 12 :
St. John, N.B.. June 12.-(Special)-A gentleman well informed on political and provincial matters, speaking to the ' World ' to-day on telephone legislation, declared incidentally that Hon. A. G. Blair was the owner of a large quantity of highly remunerative shares in the New Brunswick Telephone Company (which is practically the Bell Telephone Company). When he was Premier of New Brunswick, there was given to himself and his brother-in-law, Hon. Mr. Snowball and Hon. Senator Thompson, his son-in-law. Mr. Randolph, and other relatives (under the name of New Brunswick Telephone Company), the exclusive telephone franchise for New Brunswick, so that the Bell Telephone Company had to buy them out on coming to this province.
Hon. Mr. Blair holds one-sixth of the stock, Senator Thompson one-third, said the ' World's' informant. * The company's affairs are kept secret, but the facts became known to a few persons connected with the financial difficulties of Mr. Randolph a few years ago, in which a bank seized and sold his shares. One share of the original stock, is' now represented by three shares, each of which is held at at least 270 per cent, making about 800 per cent, of present value, at a minimum estimate.
Mr. Blair is thought to derive the largest part of his large income from this stock (which is practically Bell stock).
Asked how he thought the telephone Bill now before the Dominion House would be supported, the ' World's' informant replied :
'Senator Thompson will be about the bitterest foe of telephone reform in the Senate, although Senator MacKay is president of the Bell Company, and Senator Kirehhoffer is largely interested. Mr. Blair will exert his opposition chiefly through Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick, whose

schemes he will in turn support, such as the Quebec Bridge Company, the St. Lawrence Power Company, &c.
Now, I did not want to bring this matter before the House, but it is before the House now, it is in the public press, and it is now on tiie ' Hansard.'
Will you send the paper over to me ?
speakername: The MINISTER OE RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Yes. Under these circumstances, I say it is most unfortunate that it is the president of a company associated with tiie Bell Telephone monopoly who rises in this House and tells me, and the rest of us who are asking for some protection against the Bell Telephone Company, that we are urging something that is socialistic and doing something to disfigure a public Bill. We are doing nothing of the kind, we are doing something which we think to be in the public interest. I say it is contrary to British constitutional practice, it would not be allowed for one moment in England-for a minister to stand up in his place in the House and become the apologist of a company in which he is interested, a company from which he derives a certain portion of his income. I do not care if he did not have a dollar of income, if he merely held that stock and was interested in the company, it is against public policy that he should stand up in this House and be the apologist of that corporation. Now there has been a great deal said in this country about the conduct of our public men, and their relations to public questions, where their private interests become a question of public interest. In this matter I have based my statement altogether on the fact that the minister is the president of this company. I make no reference to other matters contained in this statement; but the mere fact of his being president of this company, and being associated with Mr. Sise, the head of the Bell Telephone Company, I say is against public policy, and it should not be allowed, and it ought to call for the minister's resignation. If the minister does not resign, the Prime Minister ought to ask him to resign. This is not an example to set before the people of this country, it is not an example to set before members of the legislature, it is not a good example to set before municipal councillors all over this country against whom charges are made that they are doing tilings in their own interest which are against the public interest. When they see tiie highest legislative body in this country, when they see cabinet ministers representing the people of Canada, when they see such things being done by a colleague of the Prime Minister, they will say that it justifies everything that has taken place in the legislatures, everything that has taken place
in township and village councils that is wrong. I appeal to the Prime Minister if it is not true that in England such a thing would not be tolerated for a moment in the House of Commons. I want to tell the Prime Minister another thing. In these paragraphs I have read, the name of a Senator in the other branch of this parliament is mentioned, a great friend of the Liberal party, Senator McKay-I suppose I can use his name as it is mentioned in the document I have read. It is a peculiar thing that the very first Senator who was appointed by this government on coming into power was the gentleman who is the present vice-president of the Bell Telephone Company, and was at that time. The name of another Senator is mentioned who has also been appointed by this government. It is a peculiar thing that in some way there is an apparent political connection between the kind of protection accorded to the Bell Telephone Company by the government, by the House, and by this committee so far; it is a peculiar thing, I say, that this company, in its monopolistic tendencies, should be specially guarded in every way.
Now, I did not wish to say this to-day, but I am forced to say it in view of the [DOT] way my amendment has been treated, in view of the way in which the Telephone Bill that I have introduced and is now before a committee of this House, is being treated. It is simply scandalous, and I will stand it no longer. I did not wish to take the stand I have taken to-day, but I am forced to take it, and I accept full responsibility for anything I have said or done. I can tell the Prime Minister that if he chooses to justify this conduct, I will be only too glad to meet him on any platform he likes to select; I especially invite him to come to West Ontario and to East York, where the people have had experience of this monopolistic treatment against the public interest, accorded to them by the Bell Telephone Company. I would like to meet the Postmaster General in his own county of North York, or any portion of Ontario. He is the Minister of Labour, the man who is going to give the farmers rural postal delivery. I am going to hold the Minister of Railways up to the British constitutional practice as observed in England, and which ought to be observed in this country. I say the Prime Minister ought to call for the resignation of his Minister of Railways in view of the simple fact I have brought to his attention to-day, that tiie Minister of Railways is interested in the New Brunswick Telephone Company as president, and that in opposing my amendment he has chosen to impute motives that he should not impute to any member who proposes something in the public interest. I leave it with the right hon. Prime Minister. I leave it with his colleagues, and I leave it with the people of Canada, to deal with it at the proper time.

My hon. friend (Mr. Maclean) must pardon me, Mr. Chairman, if I cannot take liim seriously upon this subject. My hon. friend, perhaps, has been advocating an idea which is deserving of consideration, and, for my part, I may tell him that I would have been gladly willing to have given it that consideration to which it is entitled upon its own merits.
speakername: Tlie PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier).

speechtext: I waited long enough.

My hon. friend has not at all improved the inherent merit of his position by the speech which we have listened to and by the reckless charges he has thrown out. He is not fair. He must not abuse his advantages. My hon. friend Invites me to go to East York, and he says that if I accept his invitation he will pulverize me. Mr. Chairman, I do not want to be pulverized. Why should I go to East York, where he would hold me up to the scorn of the electors, and where I would be pulverized by himself, morally, intellectually and in every other way ? We can discuss this question here without the necessity of going to East York. We can discuss . it just as well here as anywhere else. My hon. friend has said that it was a strange thing that Mr. Mackay was appointed to be a senator, and he commented upon the fact that he was a senator and president of the Bell Telephone Company. I do not know that it is a crime for anybody to be connected with the Bell Telephone Company or any other respectable company. Would my hon. friend say that it is a charge to be imputed to anybody that he is president of an enterprise that has done a great deal for the country, even though perhaps it has tried to take more from the public than my hon. friend thinks it ought to have taken ? Does he believe that lie can be taken seriously by hon. members on this side of the House, or by hon. members on the other side of the House, when advocating an idea which, as I said a moment ago, has some inherent merit in it, or does he think he is at all advancing his cause by making such silly charges as that ? Does he believe that he is to be taken seriously when he says that the government ought not to have appointed a respectable citizen such as Mr. Mackay is because it happens that he is a member of the Bell Telephone Company ? The Bell Telephone Company, my hon. friend will not deny, has been a good deal of service to the country.
Hear, hear.

Very well. My hon. friend says that it has taken too much toll from the public. That is a subject for consideration. But, at all events, I do not think the government made any mistake in calling Mr. Mackay to the Senate. If my hon. friend will take my word for it, I will tell him that I did not know that Mr. Mac-Uay. when appointed a senator, was presi-

dent of the Bell Telephone Company or that he was a member of it. That idea never entered into the consideration of the government in appointing him to the Senate. The same thing might be said in regard to Senator Thompson. It appears that Senator Thompson is a member of the telephone company, and my hon. friend says that my colleague the Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) is also a member of the telephone company. That is the first intimation I have had of it, but I do not know that it is a crime for anybody to hold the stock of such a company as that. My hon. friend says that the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals ought to resign at once and that I should call upon him to resign, because he is connected with the telephone company. I must say that the views which I hold of the ethics of xiarliament do not agree with the views held by my hon. friend in regard to the ethics of parliament. My hon. friend says that he should resign because he has been the apologist of the company, which is before this House. That company is not before this House. My hon. friend the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals would be deserving of the censure of this House if, being the president of a company, he should be made the promoter of the interests of that company. But who has brought the Bell Telephone Company into this debate ? It is not in this debate at all. This is a Bill of general interest, not for the profit or benefit of any company whatever, not for the profit or benefit of this company or of that company. It is a general Bill for the regulation of trade and commerce on railways. My hon. friend has introduced an amendment upon this subject, my hon. friend has asked parliament that what concerns the Bell Telephone Company should be grafted in this Bill, and because he has brought in that amendment declaring that that which concerns the Bell Telephone Company should be grafted in such a Bill as this, he says that forthwith the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals ought to resign. My hon. friend says that you will never find anything of the kind in England. He recalled the fact to me a moment ago that I claimed to be a Liberal of the British school. So I do claim to be a Liberal of the British school to-day, but I defy my hon. friend to bring anything forward to justify the position that he has taken.
The hon. Minister of Railways and Canals would resign if he were in England.

No such thing would take place in England. What takes place in England is this : If any member is connected with a company, he will not be allowed to promote the interests of that company on the floor of parliament, and if he does it. he is abusing the privilege of parliament ; but, when there is legislation of a general character brought before parliament, no member is prevented from voting

ov exercising the privileges of his position because it so happens that he is a member of an incorporated company. My hon. friend will not find anything in the records of the British parliament to justify his contention. My hon. friend is altogether unwarranted in the assertion he made a moment ago that the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals is the main apologist of the Bell Telephone Company. I do not know that the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals has uttered a single word either as apologist or detractor of the Bell Telephone Company. I have not followed the discussion very closely, but I am sure I am within the judgment of the House when I say that the hon. Minister of Railways and *Canals never uttered one word one way or the other. My hon. friend stated earlier in the debate that I was a Liberal. I do not know what he calls himself. I presume he is a Tory, but he told us that he was a Tory who acts as a Radical. I do not know whether he is a Radical Tory or a Tory Radical, but I rather believe that he is a Radical Tory, that he is one of those out-and-out Tories, whose instincts have always been to entrench upon the property of other people. That has been their habit in the eld land, and in this land as well. But my hon. friend will allow me in this connection to say that I have looked with some suspicion on the legislation which he has introduced upon this subject. I accuse him formally, not of being a socialist, but of being a communist. I thought there was something in his Bill that smelt strongly of communism, because he has betrayed a tendency to commit depredations upon vested rights and the property of other people. My hon. friend has introduced an amendment which I find qualifies very much the Bill which he introduced. There is in the amendment a principle which is not in the Bill which he introduced. The amendment reads :
The company shall, subject to the approval of the board, grant equal telephone entrance to its stations to all individuals or telephone companies asking therefor.
I call the attention of the committee to the words ' subject to the approval of the board.' This is a new feature which has dawned upon the mind of my hon. friend, and I must say it somewhat softens his communistic doctrines. Before that he wanted to commit a depredation upon the property of other parties outright without the qualification which he puts in now, and by which he says that this power shall be exercised only to the approval of the board. I see a great qualification in that, and if my hon. friend had proceeded differently, I would have been disposed to have taken over this amendment for future consideration.
I gave the right hon. Prime Minister every opportunity to say that.
But in view of the attitude of the hon. gentleman, and in view of the insulting language he has used towards hon. members of this House, there, is nothing to do but to vote down his amendment.

Mr. Chairman, I do not rise for the purpose of taking any part in this debate, but I wish to correct a statement which has been made, and which has been read from a paper by the hon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean), to the effect that the way they discovered who the holders of the stock of this telephone company were was that Mr. Randolph had got into financial difficulties and that the stock was sold. I do not wish this statement to go broadcast through the country in that way, because it is a well known fact in our part of the country, whether it is here or not, that Mr. Randolph was not in financial difficulties, and therefore that the stock could not have been sold for that reason.

I expected that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Maclean) would, some time during the present session, read the statement which he has read to-day, because I saw that this story was being quite generally disseminated throughout the country. I have never been In the habit, in the course of my public career, of following up slanderous and defamatory statements as they appear In the newspaper press, because I have felt that I would have very little else to do if a certain class of newspaper men thought they would be likely to receive attention if they published statements that would have a scandalous and defamatory effect. Therefore, I have taken no notice of these things ; but the hon. gentleman, having read what he has read to-day, it is only fair that I should characterize it, as I can characterize It in the main, a tissue of wholly unfounded statements. It is true that I have been the holder of stock in the New Brunswick Telephone Company. If that is a crime, I have been guilty of that crime. It is true that I have been filling, since the organization of that company, a good many years ago and a good many years before I came to Ottawa, the position of president, not that I am receiving any salary from the company, for I have not received a dollar of salary from it. I was asked to take, in an honorary way, the position of president of the company, and when I came to Ottawa I saw no impropriety in my continuing in that position, without having had anything more to do with the management of the business than I had before I came here, or as much.
I have, therefore, to acknowledge that I am open to the accusation of having been connected with the company, and of being the president of that institution. It is also a fact that Mr. Sise, a gentleman known as

Colonel Sjise, in Montreal, bolds stock in that company. But when the hon. gentleman (Mr. Maclean) says that I am interested in and connected with the Bell Telephone Company, he states what he cannot have, and has not, the slightest authority for stating. It is absolutely and entirely incorrect. I cannot tell who are all the shareholders of the company. I did at one time know who they were, but I have not seen the share list for some time. But I have known that Colonel Sise is a shareholder, quite a considerable shareholder. He took stock in the company the same as others took stock in the company, so far as I know. But I hold no stock in the Bell Telephone Company, and if, because Colonel Sise is a shareholder in another company in which I have some stock ; if that makes me a party interested financially or otherwise in the Bell Telephone Company, then I can only say that it is a very strange conclusion to draw from a very single and individually distinct fact. Therefore, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Maclean), has no warrant for saying that I have the slightest interest in the Bell Telephone Company any more than he has, perhaps not as much. I have not one dollar of stock in the Bell Telephone Company ; I have never had and never expect to have. So far as their financial interests are concerned, or so far as their interests in any way are concerned, I am as indifferent to them as is the hon. gentleman opposite ; quite as indifferent. The trouble with the hon. gentleman (Mr. Maclean) is that he cannot imagine any person can have an opinion upon any question which he raises, or upon any question of public moment, unless he be moved to that opinion through some private or personal interest of his own, or through some private or personal interest of his friends. That is the trouble with the hon. gentleman (Mr. Maclean). He cannot conceive it possible that any man, upon any public question can* have an opinion which is not subordinate to some improper motive, or which is not instigated or suggested by some personal or individual interest.
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS (Hon. A. G. Blair).

speechtext: Would the hon. minister permit me to ask him a question ?
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman think it conceivable that a minister of the Crown, having charge of a Bill ; a government Bill that might trench upon the rights of a telephone company of which he was president; is it not conceivable that he might choose in favour of the company rather than the public interest ?
What is that ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Is such a position not conceivable to the public, and a reasonable one ?

From what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Maclean) has stated, I do not think that any other telephone company in Canada could have any interest in opposing his motion except it would be the Bell Telephone Company, because the Bell Telephone Company is the company, according to his argument, upon which these monopolistic privileges have been conferred.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It would include all others would it not ?

How could it possibly include all others ? The hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) cannot have followed the discussion with any attention, or else he would see that the argument is the other way. Now, if the hon. gentleman (Mr. Maclean) had been able to show that I was a stockholder, or that I was interested in a financial way in the Bell Telephone Company, he might have some ground for imputing to me the offence with which he has charged me: of being influenced in my view of this question because I was interested in the Bell Telephone Company. But 1 am not interested in the Bell Telephone Company to the extent of a five cent piece, and, therefore, whether the Bell Telephone Company do or do not continue to en.ioy any advantages which they have derived from their contract, is a matter of complete indifference to me so far as that is concerned. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Maclean), in this statement, goes on to say that this company in New Brunswick-I will refer to that because I suppose I might as well meet the imputation now. He says:
When he was Premier of New Brunswick the stock was given to himself and his brother-inlaws. the Hon. Mr. Snowball, and the Hon. Senator Thompson.
I had no stock given to me. I paid for the stock I got; I paid for it the same as other people ; I paid for it out of my own means :
And that they had an exclusive telegraph franchise from the New Brunswick government so that the Bell Telephone Company had to buy them out on coming to that province.
Let me show the utter fallacy of that statement. The Bell Telephone Company was in New Brunswick before the New Brunswick Telephone Company had any existence. Therefore, that statement falls to the ground. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Maclean) has been deceived in the representations that have been made to him, and he has caught them up without ascertaining or attempting to ascertain whether there was any foundation for them. But, nevertheless, he comes here and he makes a cold blooded accusation against me as being guilty of a breach of my duty such as would entitle him to demand that I should resign
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
my place In tlie government of the country. He says that this company had an exclusive monopoly in New Brunswick. The company has not any exclusive monopoly at all in New Brunswick. Any other telephone company can be organized, and companies have been organized in New Brunswick. 1 will tell you what they have or what they had, lest it might be said that 1 withhold something. When the company got its charter, a great many years ago, in consideration of its building a long distance telephone, it was allowed the long distance privilege exclusively between certain towns for a term of years. They erected their lines according to the agreement between the government and the legislature and themselves but the exclusive privilege has long since expired, so that that company have no exclusive privilege, and when they had, it did not apply at all to the general telephone system in the province, because it was only a long distance privilege and did not apply to the cities and towns. He says further :
The company's affairs are kept secret, hut the fact became known to a few persons connected with the financial difficulties of Mr. Randolph a few yars ago.
My hon. friend (Mr. Hale) has answered that. So far as Mr. Randolph is concerned, although he happened, while he lived, to be connected with me, and I am connected with the family ; every one in New Brunswick knows that Mr. Randolph had no financial troubles. Neither do I think that he or his family had any stock in the Bell Telephone Company. I am not aware that they had. All this jumbling together of these statements came from some source to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Maclean)-I almost suspect I know who it is. Some person who thought he was going to get some sort of a blow at me which would be injurious to me, has communicated with the hon. gentleman- that is, supposing it is a genuine despatch, and was not made up in the office of the newspaper in which it is published. However, I am willing to admit that it was a genuine despatch. So much for that. I will leave that just where it is. I think the hon. gentleman (Mr. Maclean) ought, as n member of parliament; I think at all events as a matter of fairness he ought to have, before he disseminates and before he takes the means which will disseminate all over this country accusatory statements of that kind which are calculated to affect a public man unfavourably wherever they are read ; he ought at least to have taken some little pains to verify the correctness of these statements. He told us that he read this very reluctantly and that he would rather not have read it. I did not see very much reluctance on his part. But whether that is so or not, he did not hesitate to publish it, and probably if he felt so very much adverse to disseminating these falsehoods, he would not have been so ready to make 174
them public through the columns of his paper. I do not know whether it has a wide circulation or not, perhaps it has a limited circulation-but at all events he gave it all the circulation he could give it.
Coming now to the question before the committee. The hon. gentleman says that he waited to find out what was going to be done by the government. But the hon. gentleman heard on Saturday last what I had to say about it. I stated my view then, and I have not seen any reason to change that view from listening to the arguments that have been made. I felt that these arguments were not really addressed to the motion which is before the House. They were addressed upon the general proposition which perhaps might be put in such a form as would commend itself to parliament, but the motion in its present form is in such a state that it certainly cannot be accepted and made part of the law of the land. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Maclean) seems to be very much incensed at some bantering reference I made to his radicalism and social propensities, but I think the observation was fair enough in view of the attitude which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Maclean) has set up in this House upon so many occasions. The legislation he introduces is of such a character that I do not think any one would take the responsibility of fathering it who was a responsible individual. I stated on Saturday that I could not accept the motion introuduced by him, and i thought that was answer enough. I did not see that X was called upon to make any further reply. I stated the reasons why I could not accept it, and I think they are cogent reasons. Xle is not proposing legislation about some country districts ; he is not confining his legislation to out of the way places, but he is making his legislation general. I do not say that it would commend itself very much to my mind, even if it had been limited. He proposed :
That subject to the approval of the railway board a railway company shall grant equal telephone entries to its stations to all individuals or telephone companies asking therefor.
Now the only thing the board has to say is whether or not this law may be applied, whether or not the privilege, whenever applied for, shall be granted. They have nothing to do with the terms or conditions, as to what the telephone company ought to do or not to do in return, but what the board is asked to do is to approve of the proposition, and when they say yes, then the telephone goes in without any terms being provided.
Would not that be a matter within the jurisdiction of the com missioners under that resolution ?
What ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Do not these objections of the minister merely refer to matters of detail ?
I do not think so. Does the hon. gentleman ask us to frame an amendment for him that could be accepted ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Under the proposed
amendment the board, having the right to approve or disapprove, would insist on the terms upon which the additional telephone service would be put into the station.
The clause does not say so.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: If the board can say, you may or may not do this, does it not follow as a matter of course, that they can also say, you may do it on certain conditions ? Is not that a reasonable proposition ?

They could if they were authorized by parliament to say on what conditions that should be done; but the amendment does not say so. It does not say, upon such terms and conditions as the board may deem right to impose.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Is it not in the discretion of the board to say whether permission shall be given or not ? That being the case, if the board thinks the terms and conditions are unreasonable, they can refuse to allow the telephones to be put in.
There is no doubt they could refuse, and when they did refuse, that would be the end of it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I think the very fact that the hon. member for East York proposes to give the commission discretion, is an evidence that he does not wish to deal harshly with the railway company. I think it is only fair to point that out.

That is a matter of judgment. I think he has but one idea in his mind, that it should be imposed by law, subject to the regulation of the board, that any telephone company or any individual should have a right to put a telephone into a railway station and on the same terms. The board has not any discretion to vary the terms. There is a good deal more in this thing than most people imagine. No doubt there is on the part of a number of hon. gentlemen in this committee a feeling that it would be a great convenience in out of the way places if any telephone company doing business there were to be allowed the privilege of using the railway stations. But, after all said and done, these things can only be allowed under fair and reasonable conditions; and what have we to do with many Hon. Mr. BLAIR.
of the things that have been suggested here as reasons for granting the privilege ? One gentleman says, here is a person living ten or twenty miles away, he ought to have the privilege of calling up the agent and finding out what the market reports are. Another gentleman says that a man living at a long distance from the station, instead of being compelled to go to the station, ought to have the privilege of calling up the station agent to find out whether some friends of his whom he expects, have arrived, or when they ought to arrive. Just imagine such a proceeding as compelling the putting up of a telephone in the railway office by anybody who may ask it. I have had some little experience of these telephones on the Intercolonial Railway, and I am bound to say that they are very much of an annoyance and a nuisance. People who know the advantage that is taken of these telephones, and the circumstances under which they are used, will be quite ready to admit that this imperious demand that the railway companies shall allow telephones to be put in their offices for the convenience of everybody, has not so much reason or fairness behind it as at first sight appears. We allowed telephones to be put into some of our offices on the Intercolonial Railway, not because they were of any convenience to us, but because it was claimed that they would be a convenience to the public. What was the result ? There is quite a village and a considerable settlement in the neighbourhood. The result was that the girls and boys, the men and women, were constantly calling up and repeating their inquiries as to when such and such a train was to come in, whether so and so had arrived, whether this, that, or the other thing had happened. After they got an answer, they would call up again, keeping the station agent in the office replying to questions which in nine cases out of ten were purely for curiosity. That is how they work in many country districts. The telephones are simply made a perfect nuisance. They are not used by any means largely for business purposes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman contend that because things like that occur, which occur with the best managed telephones throughout the country, we should discount the possibility of having legitimate business done over them ? The hon. gentleman has not urged any reason
I have no objection to the hon. gentleman asking me a question, but he is making a speech.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I was going to ask the hon. gentleman this if he thinks that because he has offered simply the trifling reasons, the real and legitimate reasons ought not to be granted ?
I say the real and legitimate reasons do not exist to the extent that hon. gentlemen think.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: What answer has the hon. minister given to the statement of the hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver) respecting the condition of things that will be created in his district ?
I did not understand the hon. gentleman to say that anything very serious has occurred in his district.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: What I said was that there is a system of something over 300 phones, with three exchanges, with radial lines in three directions for about twenty miles each, and another line of about twenty miles under construction. The Bell Company have never been in that part of the country at all, but are now stringing a long distance phone from one end of the country to the other, and just as soon as that reaches Edmonton, that company will have exclusive rights to the Edmonton railway station, and the local system will be cut off if the company enforces its rights under this agreement. I can only say that such a thing would be an outrage, and I hope *that we shall be protected against it.
The Canadian Pacific Railway is not the only railway company that is going to be at Edmonton. It is the only one there at present.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The information could not be got from one railway station that could only be obtained from the other.

I do not know about that. It is very possible that any one who wanted to know something about the Canadian Pacific Railway could find it out at the other station. Why should not a railway company have a right to say what telephone it would prefer to use for its own purposes ? And why should it at the same time be compelled to admit other telephones, and to do it on the same terms ? They may be prepared to make fair and reasonable terms with the first telephone company that applies to them, and if another telephone company came along that had not any business connections and that they were not satisfied would serve them as well, why should they be obliged to admit it on exactly the same terms ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
For this very reason, that a great many people who are not patrons of the Bell Telephone Company desire to get information from the railway station ; and if a rural system, such as that referred to by the hon. member for East York and 174}
that referred to by the hon. member for Alberta, is established in these different places, they have a right, I think, to ask the government to afford them facilities at the railway stations. I am satisfied that the more the hon. minister considers this matter, the more he will realize that there is a great deal of foundation for the statement of the hon. member for East York that the public have the impression that they are being discriminated against because they are not subscribers to the Bell Telephone Company.

There is no doubt that the Bell Telephone Company has the advantage, with its extensive lines and its far reaching connections, and it makes it difficult for any other system to exist alongside of it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The telephone system is a monopoly, in its very nature, and the public are forced by the unfair exactions of that telephone company to establish other lines. These lines must be largely local, and a great deal of business done by these local lines would be done in connection with railway matters. I am sure that the hon. minister must see that if the agreement between the railway companies and the Bell Telephone Company is left undisturbed the monopoly which the Bell Telephone Company enjoys will be given a great deal longer life. The proposal is surely a reasonable one, that reasonable facilities should be given to these independent companies.

The case presented by the hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver), is a case which does seem to be somewhat serious in the possibility of its results. But the question, after all, is very much larger than the question of the interest of the people in one locality. We must not shut our eyes to the fact that we cannot under any system of legislation-perhaps we ought not to If we could-advantageously nullify or impair the strength of any company such as the Bell Telephone Company. We hear a great deal about excessive and exorbitant rates ; I do not know that the rates are ; but I do not take a great deal of stock in these complaints. People are apt to think that these things should be done for nothing. But let them put their money into such a concern
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That is exactly what they want to do.
It is the service we want. So far as the rates are concerned, I for my part, do uot object to them so much, if they will give ns the service.
Exorbitant rates and bad service go with monopoly.
I have not heard very much complaint about the Bell service. I thought it was pretty good; it is a good service here.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It may be pretty good here, but so far as the city of Toronto is concerned, it is a very bad service. Every one tells the same story.

I know they have a very up-to-date system here. You often find people coining along promoting companies and promising to do great things for the people. But the object, in ninety-nine cases out of a hundred, is to be bought out by other companies or to make a little ' pull ' out of the organization.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I am satisfied that if the hon. minister will consider the principle involved in the case, in view of the extensive powers given to the commission under the new Railway Act, he will agree that some latitude ought to be given in cases such as are mentioned by the bon. member for East York, to allow the commission to order that facilities be given to other exchanges than the Bell to put instruments into the railway stations. It is not in the public interest that the Bell Telephone Company should be permitted the exclusive privilege of placing instruments in the railway stations.

We do not give them any exclusive franchise. But I am looking at it from a railway point of view. While I am willing to keep the railways under strict control, I cannot shut my eyes to the fact that there is a disposition, and a growing disposition, throughout the country to regard the railway companies as having very slender rights, and to regard them as institutions to be jumped on. People are forgetting that, after all, though the railway companies have been granted these privileges, and even though their charter rights are very extensive, you do not find any of them in this country making a great deal of money.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: You find some people in connection with them who appear to be pretty comfortable.

Yes, but they are not the body of the shareholders. There are hundreds of shareholders outside of these people whose return is dependent upon the dividends which these companies pay. There may be some individuals who through some ' pull ' get the special benefits from the railway companies. But the great bodv of shareholders, I think, are fairly entitled to consideration.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Then the hon. minister thinks It would impair the prospects of the Mr. MACLEAN.
shareholders of the company to have the proposal of the hon. member for East York carried out ?

I cannot think it is fair play even to a railway company that you should say that any other company shall have the right, on demand, to put its telephone into the station and compel the clerks and agents of the railway company to serve those telephones.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I agree with a great deal that the hon. minister has said on that point. But I would, with all due respect to the hon. gentleman, submit to him what was said by the hon. member for East York when the matter was last discussed :
I appeal to the minister to take my suggestion and incorporate in this Bill this clause, or a clause having a similar effect.
That was evidence that the hon. gentleman was not wedded to any particular form of words in which to frame his amendment, but rather wanted to present to the hon. minister a grievance which certainly exists in certain parts of the country, and to appeal to the minister, who has given this matter so much attention and from whom the public expects so much, to take the subject into consideration and frame an amend-, ment which would vest in the commissioners the power which he thinks necessary- and which, I must say seems to me, to be plainly necessary-in cases of emergency, to allow the people to have additional telephonic communication with the railway stations. The hon. gentleman, of course, must have confidence in the proposition, which this House has affirmed on so many occasions, that the appointment of a commission will result in great good to the public.
I think it is generally considered that, if a proper commission be appointed, the public will greatly benefit from its establishment and operations. And when the hon. member for East York proposes that the terms and conditions upon which additional telephonic communication may be allowed with the railway stations shall be left to the judgment of the commissioners, the minister may rest assured, as we are all assured, that not only the public interest, but the interests of the railways, will be served. Under the circumstances, I would most respectfully appeal to the hon. minister to give the matter consideration, and not to come to a decision to-day. Consideration of this Bill cannot be completed in less than two or three more sittings of the committee, and, before it is finished, he will be able to give the matter his attention. On every side there is a rising feeling throughout the country that the Bell Telephone Company ought not to be permitted, as they are permitted, to discriminate against the great body of people who are not their subscribers, by means of their ar-

rangement with the railway companies. These railway companies enjoy great rights and privileges obtained from this parliament and from various provinces and municipalities. Many of these railways have been heavily bonused by the provinces and the municipalities. The people who pay these bonuses have some rights left, we hope. I think we can appeal to the lion minister with confidence in this matter, to give the subject his serious consideration, and, if he does so, he will assuredly arrive at a compromise that will be satisfactory to the hon. member for East York, and will, at the same time, secure to the people the rights they are entitled to.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Clarke) has certainly made a very earnest appeal but he has not a great deal of mercy.
speakername: The MINISTER OE RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I have so much mercy that I would be glad to leave the framing of the amendment in the minister's own hands.
The MINISTER OE RAILWAYS AND CANALS-if he would impose upon me the consideration of questions coming up in this way. Certainly the amendment does not come forward in a form to make it obviously sound and complete. If the hon. gentleman thinks that I can, in the time when I am putting through this Bill, and with all the questions arising in connection with it, find time to consider and frame a proper amendment on new questions, I can hardly feel that he is in sympathy with my efforts or that he is taking a wholly reasonable view* of what ought to be done.
The hon. minister has a draftsman, has he not ?

I have a very able assistant. I do not know whether hon. gentlemen have applied their minds to this whole question or not; I doubt it. But I would feel called upon to apply my mind to it before I would take the responsibility of consenting, so far as I am concerned, to this going into the Bill. I wish to point out to my hon. friend (Mr. Clarke) two or three things that I was going on to say when he rose a moment ago. I want to discuss this thing fairly. You are proposing to impose upon the railway company the duty, if it allows one telephone company to put its telephone into the office, of allowing other telephones to be put in upon precisely the same terms.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: No.
That is the proposition.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Not unless the commissioners think it right.

It is a question of yes or no.
The proposition is that the railway company shall have no right to say upon what terms telephones shall be put into their stations unless they allow other telephones in on equally favourable terms. What would be the effect ? I know absolutely from my own knowledge that it is idle to say that a station agent can attend to two or three instruments as well as to one. I believe that is good railroad opinion. I know that some of my own officers hold that opinion. I have discussed the matter with the general manager of the Intercolonial Railway and the chief engineer; and they tell me that to attempt to pay attention and reply to and follow two or three telephones, would, in many instances, be fraught with danger. The station agent's business is to follow his ticker closely; he must not allow his attention to be diverted. He may answer the telephone once in a morning, but to multiply these calls would create a possible danger. That is a thing that must be considered. I think that the passing of a clause such as the hon. member (Mr. Maclean) has proposed would result in this- that the railway company would turn out every telephone, and we should have demands made upon us that they be compelled to admit them to their offices. They serve the great majority of the people, they are a direct convenience.
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Will that cut out all the telephones ? Do you think the agent would not lose more time answering personal questions that will be asked in consequence ?

When it comes to a personal application, he would not have one question to forty lie would have to answer otherwise. That would be the result if you were to force the companies to take them in, if you did not recognize ordinary business rules that govern in these transactions. If you try by some statutory enactment to overcome the disadvantages of a departure from ordinary principles, you are sure to laud yourself in difficulty, and sure to fail. Supposing you got two or three instruments into an office, what time is the station agent going to have to attend to them all ?
speakername: The MINISTER OE RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That would be governed entirely by the regulations.
They have no power to do that, and you could not compel them to answer.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: They are not bound to answer now.

No, because it is a voluntary matter with them, it is a business matter, it is not something they have had forced upon them by outside pressure. I feel that while this may appear to be a very easy matter to dispose of, when you come to work it out, it is not so easy. I have no

objection to saying that if I hud the time at my disposal to think the matter over, 1 would see if I can make anything out of jt.
I may, before the Bill is finally disposed of. give it my attention. But if the hon. gentleman presses his amendment to-day I shall have to ask the committee to reject it.
speakername: The MINISTER OE RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I think after the suggestion of the minister the hon. member for East York might withdraw his amendment.
No, let it stand.

I wish to say a word in regard to some observations made by the Prime Minister. He seemed to recognize that there was perhaps a good deal of merit in the contention, but owing to the way in which the amendment was presented to the House, he did not feel disposed to accept it. I hope, however, that, in his generous nature, and after thinking the matter over further, he will not allow the public interest to suffer because of the unfortunate way in which the amendment was presented.

I told the Minister of Railways that I thought the amendment was worthy of consideration, but as it is drafted, I do not think it should be accepted by the committee. I think it should be now either withdrawn or voted down. But the Minister of Railways is quite willing to consider the idea.
Has the Prime Minister any objection to allowing the amendment to stand ?
I think it had better be withdrawn or voted upon.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I may say that this is not an amendment to the section, it is proposed as a separate section, so that it can be allowed to stand.

I cannot consent to withdraw my proposal. If the Prime Min-inister insists on a division now and he chooses to defeat it, he has a right to do so. As I have said, I was willing to assist the minister in every way, I invited him to take the suggestion, and if he had been a little conciliatory, things would not have come to the head that they have. I gave the Prime Minister every opportunity. If he thought the idea worthy of consideration, why did he not tell the House there was something ih it 1 But when the last moment arrived and the chairman was just about calling on the committee either to accept the amendment or vote it down, then 1 had to take measures to put the government in a penitential mood, because they are in a penitential mood now in consequence of the rather vigorous way which I had to adopt. I ask the minister and the leader of the House now, in view of all that has been said, to let my proposal stand until a later stage of the Bill. Perhaps it can be modified in some way to meet the objections of the Minister of "Railways.

It is clear it cannot stand, because it is not moved in amendment to any section under consideration, it is an independent amendment. What the hon. gentleman can do is to move it as a separate section before we get through with the Bill, and there would be no advantage taken of the fact that it is rejected as an amendment.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: An hon. member can withdraw a motion like this and reintroduce it at a future sitting of the committee; or. if the committee is favourable, he can introduce it between any other two sections.

I am willing to consider it. I may tell the hon. member for East York (Mr. McLean) that I am willing to try and get an opportunity of thinking it out. I do not think there is much in it that is capable of being worked out, though I may turn out to be wrong.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I will withdraw it on the understanding that I may introduce it again.
This is a free parliament.
But to bring it to a sense of freedom, you may sometimes have to use tbe sledge hammer.

Withdraw.
Amendment withdrawn.
On section 235,
Every company shall, as soon as possible, and within forty-eight hours at the furthest, after the occurrence upon the railway belonging to such company, of any accident attended with serious personal injury to any person using the same, or whereby any bridge, culvert, viaduct, or tunnel on or of the railway has been broken or so damaged as to be impossible or unfit for immediate use, give notice thereof to the board: and every company which omits to give such notice shall forfeit to His Majesty the sum of two hundred dollars for every day during which the omission to give the same continues.
I propose to amend by inserting after the word ' which ' the words ' wilfully or negligently.'
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I would ask the minister to abandon that amendment. It is on the same principle that we had up the other day, that is, putting the onus in 1he wrong place. Besides in this case it is not practicable. The minister will remember that the other day we had a similar question up, and after a while he conceded that it was correct to abandon the words. How is a company going to be wilful or negligent ? How can you prove the wilful negligence of the company unless you fasten the Act upon some officer of the company ? The minister will remember that a few sections back we discussed that question with regard to the way the onus was put, and the same thing applies here. * And every company which wilfully and negligently omits to give such notice shall forfeit to His Majesty ' and so on. How can you prove that they have omitted wilfully and negligently ? If you are going to enforce the penalty you ought notf to be obliged to prove? what you will have great difficulty in proving that they have done it wilfully. If the Act is ordered to be done there is negligence if it is not done and it is almost impossible to convict a man of negligently refusing to do a thing if you have to prove that he was guilty of negligence.

I cannot agree with the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lancaster). I think it would be an extremely severe piece of legislation if, where there was no negligence, or wilfulness in the matter, we were to impose such a penalty as this. I must insist upon having these words put in.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The word ' wilfully ' is in the old Act, but the word ' negligently ' is not, and the old Act has not been found to work well.
I think this will strengthen the section very materially.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The old Act required that you should prove a malicious omission. That was bad enough, but to say that they shall not be liable unless they do it wilfully or negligently would make it necessary for you to prove some kind of negligence to enable you to enforce the penalty. You could never secure a conviction.

The old section required that they should give notice within 48 hours. The section in the Bill as originally drawn provided that they should do it within 48 hours, but now, under the amendment, they have to do it immediately. There might be some meaning in having the word ' wilfully ' inserted if they had 48 hours in which to give notice, but I do not see how it is possible to contend that the words ' wilfully ' and ' negligently ' properly come into the section as it is now proposed to be amended. If the company is bound immediately after the head officer of the company has received information of the occurrence to give notice to the board, it does not seem to me that the hon. minister has any ground for contending that there is any necessity for introducing such words as ' wilfully ' or ' negligently ' into the section. There is a specified time prescribed for their doing that and if that is thought to be too short give them a longer time, but when we prescribe the time it does not appear to be well that we should introduce words which would create such a vast uncertainty in regard to the matter. As a counsel of such large experience as the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals, I need not call his attention particularly to the fact of the amount of litigation that these two words have occasioned. The uncertainty of construction and the great diffi-cultv of determining specific cases from time to time that these two words have caused afford a sufficient reason for being very careful in introducing them except where they are absolutely necessary.
^ection. as amended, agreed to.

That section 236 be amended by inserting after the word ' hoard ' on the first line the words ' may by regulations declare the manner and form in which such information and notice shall be given and the class of such accident to which the last preceding section shall apply and may declare any such information so given to be privileged and the board.'

speechtext:
I wotild like to ask the hon. minister what this will really mean when the section becomes law. As the hon. minister is aware, I have drawn his attention once or twice to the question of the frequency of railway accidents which take

place in this country and which are attended with loss of life, and I have suggested to the hon. minister the advisability of appointing an officer similar to the officers of the board of trade in England whose duty it shall he, in the case of an accident occurring, involving the loss of a human life, to proceed at once to make a thorough and complete investigation of the causes of the accident, to make a report, and if there is any negligence shown on the part of the officers or servants of the company they should forthwith be prosecuted. I think it absolutely necessary that some such provision shall be made in the law, and I would like to ask the hon. minister if this section 236 as amended will provide the necessary machinery. I would suggest that it should not be optional with the board, in case of fatal accident, whether an official shall be sent to inquire into the causes of the accident. The hon. minister lias been good enough to order an investigation into two of the railway accidents which have occurred in this country during the past six or eight months, and I am sure I can speak with confidence when I say that the reports which have been presented by the commissioners have afforded the strongest possible testimony that is required as to the necessity of having some such officer as I have suggested appointed forthwith. I would like to ask the hon. minister if he is going to provide that there shall be such an officer and that he shall act on every occasion when an accident attended with loss of life occurs ? It ought not to within the purview, or within the right, of the commissioners to say when and where an officer shall be appointed.

That is the intention. I think there should be an investigation into every accident attended with loss of life.
air. CLARKE. I understand from the amendment that the board may send an officer. I fliink it should be mandatory, that it should not be optional with the board, and that provision should be made in this Bill that in every case where loss of life results from a railway accident an official investigation should be held into the cause of the accident and a report made. Provision should also be made for the punishment of those who are derelict in their duty. The hon. - minister knows from the reports he has received from the commissioners that they give the best possible reason why action should be taken in this matter.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I agree with my hon. friend (Mr. Clarke) in that. Where an accident occurs attended with loss of life there should be an investigation. That is the intention here.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
If the section as amended makes provision for an immediate investigation and report into the cause of every rail-Mr. CLARKE.
way accident involving a loss of life, that is all that I can ask for.

That is what the section has been framed to ensure. I agree with the hon. gentleman that there ought to be in every case.
On section 238,
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I move to amend the section by striking out the words * early in July in each year ' and inserting ' in each year before the plants have sufficiently matured to seed.'
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: This section mentions thistles and other noxious weeds. The two great pests in the railway districts in Ontario are sweet clover and mustard, and they are travelling along the railways at a rapid rate. I would move that the words ' mustard and sweet clover ' be added after the word ' mustard.'
I do not know anything about the sweet clover, but I know that the wild mustard is getting to be a serious pest in Ontario.
There are different noxious weeds in different places, and I do not think that you can cover them all.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Is this sweet clover a weed ?

It is a very injurious weed. On the Canadian Pacific Railway, east of Toronto, there are miles and miles of it, and it is a perfect pest. I believe it is mentioned in the Ontario Act as a noxious weed. The special pests in our portion of the country are thistles, mustard, and wild clover, and they ought be named iu this section and destroyed by the railway companies.
It is undoubtedly a fact that this sweet clover is getting to be an unmitigated nuisance, and it seems to propagate with great rapidity.
Have you any doubt that it is a noxious weed ? If it is a noxious weed it is covered by the section.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: A person is sometimes said to be on easy street when he is in clover, but I do not- know whether this clover would be noxious or not.
The Minister of Agriculture can tell us about that.
It is a very dangerous weed.
And the Minister of Agriculture will bear me out in saying that it travels faster along the railway track than anywhere else, for what reason I cannot say.
It must have a pass.
- I would like to have It uamed in the clause because if it is named the roadmaster will tell his seetionmen to cut it down.

We might strike out the word ' thistles ' and let the section read :	' Ail
noxious weeds.'
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I am pleased that the minister lias made an alteration by putting in the words ' before the plants are sufficiently matured, to seed.' I think that is a decided improvement, but if you began to name the noxious weeds I am afraid you will make your law weaker instead of strengthening it. If you say all noxious weeds you will include them all.

In the seed Bill of the Minister of Agriculture which is supposed to include all noxious weeds he does not mention the sweet clover, and if a question arose as to whether it was a noxious weed or not, that might be taken as an authority. This weed is sweeping widespread over the western part of Ontario and' it certainly is a great nuisance.
Sweet clover may not be classed *as a noxious weed, and therefore it should be mentioned in the clause.
You could strike out the word ' thistle ' and make it read ' all noxious weeds.'
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I would not approve of that because the thistle is not commonly called a weed, and if you do not name it I am afraid it would not come under the operation of the clause. The thistle has different characteristics from a weed, and there was no doubt a good reason for inserting it in the clause before. I would be in favour of retaining the word ' thistle ' and also including sweet clover and wild mustard.
I would not set my opinion against that of the hon. member (Mr. Henderson) as to whether the thistle is a weed, but I think it is generally regarded as being injurious to land.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Sweet clover is a very obnoxious weed and while I believe it is not included in the Bill of the Minister of Agriculture, yet it is included I think in the Ontario Act.

1 think
it would be very offensive to Scotchmen and their descendants if you were to call the national emblem of their great country a weed. I may say that in our Peoples' Garden, at Halifax, of which we are very proud, as being perhaps the best for its size in the Dominion of Canada, it is cultivated and kept as an ornament; and I feel very much hurt myself that you would place that emblem of that great and glorious country in the class of weeds.
Some thistles are comparatively harmless, such as the Scotch thistle, the Sow thistle, and the Russian thistle. The Canada thistle is the most harmful.
The Sow thistle and the Russian thistle are just about as bad as the Canada thistle.
In the Minister of Agriculture's Bill regulating the sale of seeds, the Canada thistle is specially mentioned.

I think we had better make the clause read :	' Every company shall
cause thistles and all noxious weeds,' &c.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

I propose to move the following as subsection 3, of this clause :
Every company shall also, by a sufficient number ot its employees to ensure the safe carrying out of the same, from time to time and as often as occasion therefor arises, and at the season of the year appearing to be the most safe and suitable for carrying out the work, burn or otherwise destroy or dispose of, all dry grass, weeds, decayed and decaying matter of every kind, and all waste material, refuse and rubbish, upon their right of way and lands, so as to prevent as far as possible fire accidentally originating upon and spreading from such right of way or lands, to the prejudice of the owners and occupiers of adjoining lands; and for every day during which the company neglects to comply with the provisions of this subsection, it shall incur a penalty of two dollars, to be recovered with costs in any court of competent jurisdiction, by any interested person suing therefor.

We are not at present dealing with the fire clauses. If there is any question of cutting out the long dry grass beside the track, there will be discussion of that question on a motion which is to be moved by one of the hon. gentlemen from the west. Perhaps that will be the more appropriate occasion.

speakername: The MINISTER OF JUSTICE (Hon. Charles Fitzpatrick).

speechtext: We have so often refused this power, that it seems scarcely right that we should allow it to one company, having refused it to so many others.

speechtext: I think that in view of the remarks of the hon. Minister of Justice and of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals, perhaps the Bill had better be held in committee for further inquires on the point referred to. May cause all things to he done which the said company is so required to do, and for that purpose may enter by himself, and his assistants or workmen, upon such lands, and may recover the expenses and charges incurred in so doing, and the said penalty with costs in any court of competent jurisdiction.

In connection with the question of fire ori-

ginating from locomotive engines I think one of the great sources of clanger will be eliminated if something on this line is adopted requiring railway companies, as they do already in many instances, to my knowledge, to clean up their lines of railway by the burning of grass and of such material as is useless. On section 240,
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

On section 242,
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
All these by-laws of the company are made subject to the approval of the Governor in Council, except such as relate to tolls. I would suggest that the time-tables of the company, with regard to
the arrival and departure of trains, be made subject to the approval of the board, as is the case in England, instead of the Governor in Council. There it is impossible for a railway company arbitrarily to change the time of the arrival and departure of trains, and I think the public should be in a position to appeal to the board of commissioners in a matter of this kind. Sometimes a railway company makes a radical change in its time table without consulting the public or giving the public an opportunity of being heard.

There are a good many other matters besides the arrival and departure of trains, and it might be well that the Governor in Council should determine whether or not these by-laws should be finally approved. Under section 245 the board must report upon them to the Governor in Council. The Governor in Council cannot act without such report, and you are practically reaching the same end as if you distinctly provided that they should be first submitted to the board.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It is a round-about way. The practice in Great Britain is for the public to go straight to the board of trade and be heard. There are many parts of this country through which the railways run which at times do not get a sufficient railway service ; many of the trains run through and do not stop. If there were some kind of appeal straight to the commissioners, it would save the Council a lot of trouble, and be of substantial advantage to the publie. In England the railways cannot change their time-tables radically without the municipalities or other parties interested being heard. I merely throw out the suggestion.
The arranging of the time-tables is a very much more serious matter in England, where they carry millions where we only carry thousands.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I wish to call Hie minister's attention to another matter. There is no legal connection between the insurance company and the railway. company.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I know they are quite distinct. But the company make certain

rules as a railway company, and then there are certain rules of the insurance company. Of course, I should not be right in saying that the railway was an insurance company too. I think that as a rule they are voluntary associations.

speechtext:

speechtext:
What is the meaning of
' executive officer ' in that case ? That is pretty broad.

The company or the directors of the company, by by-law, or any such officer or officers of the company as are thereunto authorized by by-law of the company or directors, may from time to time prepare and issue tariffs of the tolls to be charged, as hereinafter provided, for all traffic carried by the company upon the railway, or in vessels, and may specify ihe persons to whom, the place where, and the manner in which, such tolls shall be paid.

speechtext: I move to amend this section by striking out from subsection 4 the words ' nor until the provisions of this Act have been complied with.'
