It would be unfair to say that because the company had not cleared up the right of way according to the requirements of the Act or because they had not repaired some small bridge on a branch line-questions having nothing to do with this question of tolls-they shall not be allowed to charge.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: No.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I am not prepared to say that the hon,. minister is not right in proposing to strike out these words. There is a good deal of 'force in his suggestion. The reference in this section is to sections 223 and 231 of the old Act. It is not easy

to trace them, because there is a good deal of change in the arrangement.
Section 223 begins in this way :
Subject to the provisions and restrictions of this Act in the special Act contained.
Now that is not in any part of this section. Section 251 of this Bill begins :
The company or the directors of the company, by by-law, or any such officer or officers of the company as are thereunto authorized by by-law of the company or directors, may from time to time

It is not made subject to the provisions of this Act we are now passing, or subject to the provisions of the special Act. I submit that both of these ought to be in. I am not sure but that the provisions of this Act may be controlled by what appears down at the end of the section, but so far as the special Act is concerned, I think it ought to be in. Then there is another matter that is not in this section, which I think ought to be referred to in a foot-note, that is section 227, the provision as to the inability of the company to collect tolls. The corresponding provision, I think, is found in section 237, of the old Act, although it is not referred to :
No toll shall be levied or taken until the by-law fixing such tolls has been approved of by the Governor in Council, or until after two weekly publications in the ' Canada Gazette ' of such by-law and Order in Council approving thereof, nor shall any company levy or collect any money for services as a common carrier except subject to the provisions of this Act.
I want the minister to tell us whether he intends to leave out the provision as to the publication in the ' Canada Gazette,' or whether it is controlled by some other section.

The hon. gentleman will find that very ample provision has been made for publication. He is now dealing with a portion of the Bill which I regard as one of its cardinal features, and which is based upon a totally different principle from the existing law. What he would have me put in has been left out in accordance with the scheme on which this Bill has been designed. It would be very inappropriate, and would only serve to confuse most men, and lead to misapprehension. If the hon. gentleman will compare this Bill with the old Act, he will see that they are absolutely dissimilar. So far as this class of cases is concerned, there are twenty-five or thirty new sections. The scheme of the present Bill is not, as it is in the old law, that the railway company shall fix and regulate the tolls subject to the Railway Committee of the Privy Council. In this Bill all the railway company is authorized to do is to prepare and- issue a tariff. The words 'fixing and regulating tolls' are not to be found in any of the powers vested in the
company, but they are to be found in the powers which are conferred upon the board, subject, of course, to the approval of the Governor in Council.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I think the minister misapprehends what I was aiming at. I was merely asking the minister to explain to us if it was now necessary that the publication should be had as before. I raised a question as to the effect of the special Act on the question of tolls. I think probably that should be made more clear in this Bill. I am not sure that it might not be controlled already by some of these sections. Now suppose that we pass here a special Act in which the western members are interested. They are greatly exercised over the question of tolls, and in granting charters they often raise the question of what the tolls shall be. There have been special provisions as to tolls, and when the Grand Trunk Pacific Act is completed and a guarantee is entered into by the government, then I apprehend there will be a special provision as to tolls incorporated in the Act. So it may happen that there will be a case where a special Act will govern and control the tolls. Well, if the special Act touches that question of tolls in any existing or future charter, then it would be in unfortunate conflict with this section, because it is left absolutely in the power of the board to deal with the question of tolls.

We are proposing here, so far as language will do it, that all the powers necessary in order to govern the rates shall be possessed by this board. I would not like to introduce anything that would cast any doubt or suspicion at all on the ample character of the powers of the board in that respect.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The board can revise the tolls either up or down. Now if a railway company had a special Act in which these rates are fixed by charter and these rates were lower than the board proposed to determine, then the special Act would govern. I think I have proposed a proper precaution, and having called the attention of the minister to it, I am willing to leave the point.
There should be a notice given to the general public of the intention to issue a new tariff of tolls.
The public may come before the board afterwards.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: After it is crystallized into a tariff it is more difficult to get the board to change it than it would be if the public had an opportunity of assisting the board in the formation of it.

The public may appear before

the board, and if they make out a ease the board may make any changes that are necessary.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Notice should be given that the tariff is going to be published, so that both parties would be heard-the parties interested in having the freight rates as low as possible and the railway companies, for and against-as to the fairness of the tariff proposed. It seems to me that that would be prudent. In that way persons interested would be heard, and would be able to assist the board in making up what would be a fair rate.	,.

The publication in the ' Gazette ' is publication of the official decision at which the board has arrived. The publication throughout the country of notice of the tariff that is proposed to be submitted would impose a most onerous obligation upon the railway company. It would be a tremendous business having people coming from all parts of "Canada to be heard before the board, as well as the railway companies or their representatives, and discussing the question of rates. You must assume that the board will be advised by competent people as to what is a fair and reasonable tariff. It may be, after they have come to a conclusion, that in respect to some portions of the tariff there will be complaints. Well, the number .of people that would have any complaints to make would, ordinarily speaking, be very few. They would make their complaints before the board, and the board would cause them to be Investigated. The board would have their tariff officer make an inquiry, perhaps go to the locality from which the complaint comes, and get all the information to enable the board to say whether there should be any change made in the tariff or not. I would not like to insert a provision in the Bill that notice should be published.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
When the tariff is required to be published in the ' Canada Gazette,' why not publish notice of application for the sanction of the tariff that is proposed also in the ' Canada Gazette ' ? It would not be necessary for every person who is aggrieved or who has a fault to find in connection with the proposed tariff to come to Ottawa, or wherever the board sits, to make his complaint known. We know very well that this is done by committees and by the representatives of the parties complaining, and they could do it as easily on a proposed tariff as on a tariff that had been promulgated by the board. It seems to me that it would be a much more satisfactory way of doing it, and if, after a certain required publication, there were no complaints, the tariff would go into operation as an absolute tariff. This would be done in just the same way as you make up the voters' lists. You Hon. Mr. BLAIR.
publish your preliminary list, which is notice. It is only published in three or four places in each district, but this is notice to the public, complaints are heard, changes are made and the final list is made up and published. So, in this case. Notice of the tariff is published in the official * Gazette,' and if there are no complaints the tariff goes, while if there are complaints, those who complain can appear before the board and have the tariff revised.

I propose to have control through this board of the rates, but I do not propose to burden unreasonably or unfairly the railway companies of the country. We want to secure that control with the least possible amount of friction.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: What difference would there possibly be in allowing these complaints to be heard before the tariff was finally completed and making them after it was absolutely completed ? You say that you allow the public to go before the board if they have any grievances, and that the board has power to make changes. Why not allow the people to go before the board before the tariff is finally completed, and have their complaints heard ? It would not impose a greater burden on the railways to have that hearing before the final revision rather than to have the people heard afterwards. Would it not, as a matter of fact, be less of a burden, because then there is a certain limit of time during which applications for revision might be made ? All complaints would have to be filed before the board before that time expired.

I cannot see that there is any advantage in adopting the hon. gentleman's suggestion.
On section 252,
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I move to insert in subsection 4 of section 252 the following :
No company shall, except In accordance with the provisions ot this Act directly or indirectly pool its freights or tolls with any other railway or common carrier, nor divide its earnings nor any portion thereof with any other railway company or common carrier ; nor enter into any contract, arrangement, agreement or combination to affect or which may affect any such result.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: If you leave subsection 2 as it is, I think it is discriminating against the small shipper in the same line.

The question has occurred to me as to whether there is any conflict between subsection 2 and subsection 3. Subsection 2 provides that the tolls for longer distances may be proportionately less than the tolls for shorter distances if such tolls are under substantially similar circumstances charged equally to all parties; and
5570

subsection 3 provides that no tolls shall bo charged which unjustly discriminate between different localities. Is there any conflict between these two sections in the opinion of the minister ?

My view is that there is no conflict between them. The third subclause would not have reference to the idea that for the shorter distance you might charge a less toll proportionately. You cannot on a line 100 miles long impose a toll on freight carried fifty miles of that distance, greater than you charge for hauling it the whole distance.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It means that you cannot charge for a part more than you charge for' the whole.

Subsection 2 seems only to amount to this :	That if on a certain
part of the line they are carrying freight for say 100 miles, upon another portion of the line they shall charge substantially the same rates both being in the same direction. Take two branches converging towards one point and branch A is 100 miles distant from a common point B, the same, the circumstances being similar, they shall charge the same rate.	.
If the conditions are the same and the element of competition is absent.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It takes into consideration the quantity as well. If one man ships two carloads of grain and if another ships twenty carloads the man who ships the twenty gets the advantage. It has always been a bone of contention that the large shipper has a substantial advantage over the smaller shipper. I can understand making a reduction for quantities.

There is no doubt that this is a very controversial question. The business of carrying freight on railroads has taken certain forms and we must need be on our guard lest we disturb the business conditions to a degree that would be injurious. Since the law relating to railways has existed we have had that principle recognized by legislation, and while I can see that some argument can be made against the principle yet when we come to work it out we do not know to what it ultimately might lead. There does seem to be good reason for giving the shipper of a whole train load a lower rate than if he only shipped half a carload.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I can understand that if you ship a whole train load of cattle you get a rebate, but no matter how many cars you ship if it is less than a train load you get no rebate.

The difficulty is in arbitrarily saying that you shall not charge any less 175
proportion whether you are carrying a very large quantity or a proportionate quantity less. The special car rates are the rates which are likely to cause most trouble.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: You substantially recognize the right of the large shipper to an advantage over the small one. This Bill says that the tolls for larger quantities may be proportionately less than the tolls for smaller quantities.
It does not say that they shall be, but that they may be, and the board will consider all this.
When it says may, it practically means shall. That is what we are told by the lawyers.

After all, is that not one of the conditions of trade which we cannot very well govern here ? To my mind, the question for the small shipper is not so much whether the large shipper gets a better rate than he does, but whether he gets a fair rate himself. I claim that it would not be fair to tie any company down to give to a man who gives them hundreds of carloads to ship in a year no better rate than they would give to a man who probably gives them one carload. That do?s not seem a fair proposition, and the root of the matter seems to me to be, does the small shipper get a fair rate for the goods he ships ?
That is plainly discrimination.
I do not think it is.

If you give a better rate to the large shipper than to the small shipper, you discriminate in favour of the large shipper as against the small. I will give you an instance of how it works. A man may be shipping peas. The man who ships them in large quantities gets a lower rate, and is enabled to pay one or two cents more per bushel than another man, and in that way he can destroy" the other's trade, no matter what he does.
An lion. MEMBER. That is all the better for the farmer.

No, it is not, because he drives the small purchaser out of the market, and then he pays what he likes. There should be no discrimination between the two shippers unless it is in train load lots. It seems to me that the man who fills one car is entitled to the same rate as the man who fills six or seven, unless he makes a full train load, in which case I think he should be allowed some rebate. This was one of the means adopted by the Standard Oil Company to crush out all the smaller dealers until that company had the control of the market, and then they put up the price to suit themselves. It is to avoid



such things that we should have some control over this matter.

Ill the endeavour to exercise what we call a rigid control over the rates, you must be careful that you are not going to disturb unnecessarily or seriously the business conditions of the country. I know not in what form you could better secure the proper measure of control over the adjusting of rates as between the large shipper and the small shipper than you do by saying to the board that they may for so and so charge proportionately less. Who is to judge what may be the proper allowance or proportion of reduction ? It is the board, and their decision is absolute, subject only to an appeal to the Governor in Council. You must apply your mind to the existing facts and circumstances, taking everything into account, and you cannot frame your legislation safely, it seems to me, in any other way than you have it here. I realize as well as the hon. gentleman does what is the nature of the public grievances. There are many complaints, but many of them are very unreasonable. You could not possibly give them the relief they ask unless you were absolutely to destroy the business of the country done by the railway companies. Recognizing that these things are subject to a great deal of complaint. I have been thinking it out as well as I could, with the assistance of persons not at all interested in railways, and I have been unable to see how we could safely say that there should be no less rate charged upon a large quantity than upon a small quantity. I think you would find in practice that that would not work out even to the advantage of the small shipper. It is wholly impossible for you to legislate in such a way as will deprive the man of large means and resources of the advantage which he possesses over the man of small means and small resources.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It is because he has it in so many other ways that we desire to prevent him having it here. Parliament has laid down the principle, and the board is expected to apply that principle. 1 know that this complaint is made again and again. The larger purchaser gets special rates over the small purchaser, and in ad* dition to that he gets such an advantage iu the matter of freight rates that the other man is forced out of the market. 1 have heard this complaint over and over again, although it has been repeatedly affirmed by the railway companies that there was no discrimination. This section practically admits the principle, and it would be an instruction to the board to act upon that principle.
What the hon. member says is quite correct; this subject has been discussed again and again. It has been dis-

cussed for a quarter of a century, and if we sat here for a week and heard arguments on one side and on the other, we would not be an inch further advanced towards an agreement. The only result would be that if we passed a law absolutely preventing what this clause permits the board to allow, we would inevitably destroy 'our through business, and there would not be a ship coming to a Canadian port for traffic.
Might I remind the bon. gentleman that I said distinctly, that I did not ask you to apply it to distance ?

It is not merely a question of distance. Every week the large railway companies have got to All ships. Rightly or wrongly the ship must be filled or she would have no ballast, and would have to lie in harbour empty; and the next time you wanted that ship, she would not come to your port. The great shipping business cannot be carried on as the ordinary retail business of the country is carried on. You might as well say that a wholesale merchant should be compelled to charge as much for a hundred tons of goods as the small merchant charges for a small quantity. This subject has been discussed over and over again, and parties will never agree upon it. The only way, it seems to me, is to have a board such as is provided here; let both parties go before that board and argue the case out; get the rules established, and they will be competent to deal with this question, having the opinion of experts on one side and on the other.
Is not the combined intelligence of parliament equal to the combined intelligence of a board ?
Certainly not.

The wisdom of parliament which makes the law which controls the board, ought certainly to be equal to that of the board that is so controlled. The fact that we cannot agree for some time is no reason why we should not try to reach a conclusion. Otherwise, we might as well refuse to consider about three-quarters of the Bills that come before us. In time, and after consultation, sve reach conclusions though at first it seems impossible to do so. I do not see any harm in bringing this matter to the attention of the committee. 1 speak after years of experience in this House, when I say that I have heard it most positively stated in the Railway Committee and on this floor that legally the company could not do that. This has been stated by men who might fairly be regarded as railway experts, eminent lawyers and old parliamentarians. I am only asking to have the principle embodied in the law which I have been told actually rules-that there shall be no discrimination.
No unjust discrimination.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: What the minister may consider unjust I may consider just. But discrimination results always in freezing out the small shipper, buyer or dealer. 1 have heard it so often argued on behalf of the railways that this is not done, that it is a matter of surprise to me to hear it declared not only that it can be done, but that you must change the system in order to avoid it.

Cases differ so much that it is impossible for the House to lay down a general rule, and so it leaves it for the board to arrange. The board are seized of the circumstances of this case, and can decide each case by itself. If you have a fair board, I do not think there wiil be any difficulty in preventing unjust discrimination. We expect discrimination in favour of the large operator against the small one. That is necessary in trade. The only thing is to prevent unjust discrimination, and that can be prevented by the board considering each individual case.

That reasoning does not appeal to me. Suppose there are two men shipping wood from the station of the town in which I live. One has a rate of 32 per cord to Toronto while the other must pay 32.25. The second man simply cannot remain in the trade and compete with the other. The result is to freeze out the small shipper, give the control to one man and then he pays what he likes.
The commission would deal with a matter of that kind.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It is just like the large fish eating up the small ones-it is the law of the survival of the fittest operating here as in everything else.

I have listened with great attention to the remarks on both sides on this subject. The hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) is recognized as an expert in these matters, and I am not going to discuss the points that have been raised. But I would like the minister to give me a little information. We are supposed to be improving the law as compared with the old law. Will the hon. minister please point out what those improvements with regard to this matter are ? We are substituting a board for the Railway Committee, and, of course, I recognize that that is supposed to be an improvement. But, apart from that, how do we overcome to any extent, the evil that has been complained of in the past ? I have no doubt there is a great deal to be said on both sides as to a proper remedy, and as to whether discrimination should be allowed in any instance. I assume that the hon. minister, having given 175J
his attention to this matter, has succeeded to a certain extent, at all events, in dealing with the difficulties experienced in the past and that those difficulties will not be so great as they have been.

One radical change is made in a matter that lies at the bottom of the trouble that has been experienced in the past. 1 am not going to say that we have reached a perfect remedy for existing difficulties, because we know that perfection is not to be looked for, and we know that there is no more complicated problem in the world than the problem of railway tariffs and rates. The existing law is based upon the theory that the railway companies shall fix and regulate tolls subject to approval. All that the Governor in Council can do is to say that the tolls proposed shall not receive approval, and that is an extremely drastic course for any government or for any tribunal to adopt. They have not the power to reduce a toll from say $1.10 per ton to 75 cents a ton between certain points. They cannot make such changes as that. But under this law the board will have the absolute right to fix the toll in all cases, with one exception, which we shall come to later on, and which I shall endeavour to explain.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Would it not help it out to add to subsection 2, ' provided that there shall not in any case, be any unjust discrimination ' ?

That is the very basis of these clauses-that there shall not be any unjust or unreasonable discrimination. I refer to section 253. There could hardly be anything broader than that. The words are 'undue or unreasonable preference or advantage' and undue preference is wThat is complained of. The language is that used in the English statutes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: But when the section forbids undue discrimination in any respect whatever, does that not apply only to things mentioned there ?

That is not singled out in that clause. The language here is that which is used in the English statute and has been declared by the courts to forbid unjust discrimination, undue preference or advantage in any shape or form, in regard to rates and tolls as well as anything else.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Then why keep these words ' in any respect whatsoever,' if the same words above apply to everything ? If these words in line thirty are intended to cover every kind of preference or undue discrimination, then why do you repeat them afterwards ? In the first place, you start out to particularize, and then you add a

general statement which is supposed to cover everything that is not mentioned in the particular statement, that is, that the words ' in any respect whatsoever ' do not apply to the interchange of traffic, in receiving, forwarding and delivering traffic, but they apply to every conceivable thing in connection with traffic. Then if they do, I say it is wholly unnecessary to repeat them. But my contention is that these words ' in any respect whatsoever' only apply to affording proper legal facilities for receiving, forwarding and delivering traffic.

I do not understand what the hon. gentleman is driving at.
Sush tolls may be either for the whole or for any particular portions of the railway ; but all such tolls shall always, under substantially similar circumstances and conditions, be charged equally to all persons, and at the same rate, whether by weight, mileage or otherwise. in respect of all traffic of the same description carried in or upon a like kind of cars, passing over the same portion of the line of railway : and no reduction or advance in any such tolls shall be made in favour of or against any particular person.
There is the very first section under the head of discrimination. Now does that or does it not say that there shall not be discrimination ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
The very thing we are trying to get at is permission of the board to allow discrimination at all. The whole gist of this paragraph is to allow the board to discriminate. The point I want to make is this :	You want to provide, not that
there shall be no discrimination-because it may be right sometimes that there should be discrimination in the interests of trade- but that there shall be no unjust discrimination, which is an entirely different thing. So if you add those words and provide that there shall be no unjust discrimination, you completely cover the ground. The words in section 253 do not supply that sufficiency.

We say that as to this one limited particular, the tolls may be proportionately less for larger than for smaller quantities if the board thinks it would be reasonable and proper to make such allowance.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: But they have power to make unjust discrimination under this Act.
They may commit' errors, their judgment may be fallible.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 254, subsection 3,
3. In any case in which the toll charged by the company for carriage, partly by rail and partly by water, is expressed in a single sum, the board, for the purpose of determining

whether a toll charged is discriminatory or contrary in any way to the provisions of this Act, may require the company to declare forthwith to the board, or may determine, what portion of such single sum is charged in respect of the carriage by rail. 61 V., c. 22, s. 2 Am.
Does it mean that the board may determine without hearing the company ?
They would hear the company, I presume, on a question of this kind before they decided it, but if the company did not want to make a declaration the board might determine.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Why do you not say ' and may determine ' instead of ' or may determine ? '
I do not think that would make any difference.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: By inserting the word ' and ' you would require the company to make a declaration and if the company did not make a declaration the board would determine.
Is this clause the same as it is in the statute ?
Yes, and it was very well understood at the time it was enacted.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
It is very unsatisfactory, because you ask the company to declare, and it may make a very preposterous declaration. It is the hoard that should determine.
Mr. FOWLER, Yes ; you say ' and may determine,' even though they get a declaration of the company.
Suppose the company do not make a declaration ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: If you have the word ' or ' in, it seems to me they could determine without a declaration from the company, which might not be fair.
It might be a proper thing to do.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Yes, but it would prevent any unfairness to the company if the board requires them to make a declaration. By using the word ' and,' the final adjustment of the matter is in the hands of the board, irrespective of what the company may declare.
I want the minister to explain to the committee what the meaning of ' in the interest of the public ' is in subsection 2.

I think it will be conceded at

once that It is a very proper consideration for the board as to whether or not the public interests are to be affected favourably or unfavourably by the reduction of the tolls. You project a railway into a district where perhaps some particular class of industry cannot, in its initial stages, pay the same proportionately high rates as are imposed on the same kind of goods on the same railway in other directions. With a little assistance from the railway in the way of a diminution of the tolls, the establishment might be brought up to a paying standard and able to bear the ordinary toll. It seems to me a very proper thing for the board, not to consider the interests of the railway company alone, although it may very well do that, but to consider the public interest and the advantages to the community, and the board might very well be invested with jurisdiction to allow exceptional treatment. That is the idea we had in our minds in using that language.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I see it perfectly clearly now, and I quite concur in the view of the minister.

There is another aspect in which that is a reasonable clause. It sometimes happens that there is a large amount of perishable freight on a part of the line, and unless that could be all moved at once and the cars given to that district in preference to another, that freight would be destroyed.
On section 255,

This is another instance in which there is a material distinction between the existing law and the present Bill. The existing law provides that the freight classification shall be settled by the railway companies. The Governor in Council now possesses only the negative power to say that they will not approve. Under this Bill it is in the power of the board of railway commissioners to take articles out of one classification and to put them in another. Practical railroad operations show that after all the power to control the freight classification is largely a power which affects the rates, and that power is fully conferred upon the board of railway commissioners by this Bill. I move to add as subsection 4 :
Until the board otherwise orders or directs, the freight classification last approved by the Governor in Council before the passing of this Act shall continue in force ; and any freight classification in use in the United States may, subiect to such order or direction, be used by the company with respect to traffic to or from the United States.
The first portion of this clause will not provoke any comment, but as to the United States, it happens in actual practice that the United States freight classification controls all traffic which is brought from that country into this, or taken from this country into that; both ways. If it came out of the United States and went*through Canada and into the United States, it would be all subject to the control of the United States rates. There are four classes of freight classification in the United States, and the one which obtains in the west is different from the one which obtains in the east, but it would be impossible for our railways to carry any freight unless it meets with the requirements of the United States freight classification. They simply dominate, and there is nothing we can do to prevent that control continuing.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Does that apply to goods coming from an American point and going to a point within Canada ?
It applies in both cases.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: This amendment does not mean that when this present classification will be changed it shall be changed with respect to the United States as well ?
Unless the board orders. It is hoped that possibly some modification may be effected at a later date in respect to the action of the United States railroads.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: And you provide that the board may meet that occasion ?

In reference to the wording of the section, I am not quite sure that it bears out what the minister intends, if you should put a narrow construction on it. Narrowly construed, ' to and from the United States ' would mean the boundary line.

I do not think so. I think that refers to all the traffic, even traffic which comes through Canada and enters into the United States again, because it is from or to. A point at the boundary line must be either in one country or in the other.
On section 258,
The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS moved that this section be amended by adding thereto, at the end of the section, the following words :-
And in estimating the tolls to be charged in passengers' tariffs, any fraction of five cents less than two and one-half cents, shall be waived by the company, and above two and one-half cents shall be considered as five cents by the company.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Amendment agreed to, and section, as amended, agreed to.
On seetiou 261, subsection 3,
3.	Until the company files its standard freight tariff or tariffs as the case may be, with the board, and such tariff or tariffs is, or are, so approved and published, and also published In the manner in section 274 in such case provided. no toll shall be charged by the company.

This would require, under section 274, that the tariff shall be posted in every station. And, if the railway should happen to fail to have the tariff posted in any one of possibly hundreds of offices, they could not recover tolls. They may intend to have it posted, and actually have it posted so far as they know, but the omission to post it in any one office would prevent them from recovering their tolls. I move that this be amended by striking out the words 1 and also published in the manner in section 274 in such case provides.'
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Could it not be provided that they should not be allowed to recover tolls from the particular station in which the tariff was not posted? Section 2 provides that every standard freight tariff, on approval by tiie board shall be published by the company for two consecutive weeks in the ' Canada Gazette.' Here is where, I think, the provision should be made for a preliminary tariff.
The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS ANI) CANALS. We threshed that out, and I cannot agree with my hon. friend's (Mr. Fowler's) view. *

I suppose there is no use in urging this point further upon the minister. As to the point of publication in the station to which the hon. minister has just referred, I think there is a good deal in what he has said. But I think it is important that there should be a rule, and an almost invariable rule, that the tariff shall be posted in this way. So, while the provisions should be less drastic, there should be some provision on the subject.
Under section 274 they are required to post the tariff, and a penalty is provided in case they fail to do so.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I think that will cover the case. The point is to secure the public.

Does the hon. minister propose to sit very late to-night ?
I think I will not ask the committee to sit beyond twelve o'clock to-night.

On section 269,
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
The foreign traffic business is a business which we are bound to encourage, and the amendment suggested in this section has that end in view. Suppose a shipper in Chicago wishes to send a train load of grain to Montreal; the rate in respect to that has got to be made on the minute. The shipper is perhaps applying to a dozen different railways to know what rate they will give and he may go to a Canadian, dompany and. say :	Can you
make me as good a rate as the others have offered, and the Canadian company has to make its rate right away. You must recognize that there may be a relaxation of the strict rule that is maintained with legat'd to the ordinary traffic.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: 1 agree with every word the minister has said, but what strikes me as preposterous, is that such language should ever have crept into the original section.
We are always learning.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

This is such an excellent improvement that I think it must have emanated from this side of the House, although I suppose the minister will not give us credit for it.
